explanation: Venus's thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat, keeping its surface near 464 °C, hot enough to melt lead. Airless Mercury swings from about 430 °C by day to minus 180 °C at night.

claims.text: The mean surface temperature of Venus is about 464 °C.
The mean surface temperature of Mercury is about 167 °C.
Venus has a thick atmosphere, mostly carbon dioxide, that traps heat at the surface.
Lead melts at about 327 °C, well below the surface temperature of Venus.
Mercury has almost no atmosphere, and its surface reaches about 430 °C by day and falls to about minus 180 °C at night.

writerNotes: Self-check (CONTENT_GUIDE 9.3). lint: content:check run on the batch; see the batch result. claims: every statement in the labels and explanation is listed; c1, c2, c4 and c5 hold numbers, so they are high under C26; c1 and c2 are the label claims of a counterintuitive item. datasets: ptable gives lead a melting point of 600.61 K (Lead, melt), which is about 327 °C, for c4. No pinned dataset covers planetary temperatures, so I spent one writer search on c1 and c2: query 'NASA planetary fact sheet mean surface temperature Mercury 167 C Venus 464 C'; results included nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov (Mercury Fact Sheet, Planetary Fact Sheets) and science.nasa.gov (Temperatures across our Solar System); the summary said NASA pages give Mercury's mean surface temperature as 167 °C and Venus's as 464 °C, and noted third-party figures of 467 °C and 477 °C for Venus, both still far above Mercury. rivalTest: Mercury is closest to the Sun, so most players pick it; that is the trap. Against the key: Mercury's daytime peak (about 430 °C) is still below Venus's mean, and the stem asks about the average, so no reading makes Mercury hotter. The ratio 464 to 167 clears the 1.1 guard easily. volatility: evergreen. regional: planetary science taught everywhere. style: Oxford spelling, no dashes (I wrote 'minus 180' rather than a sign), explanation 34 words. myths: claims screened against content/reference/myths.json; the item debunks mercury-hottest-planet in spirit, but no claim uses the word 'hottest', so C25 should not fire. mystery and encore: not applicable. doubts: c5's night figure is often given as minus 173 °C or minus 180 °C; I used 'about'. stem: Which planet's surface is hotter on average?

evidence.restatement: Venus's average surface temperature is roughly 464 degrees Celsius, about 737 kelvin, the hottest of any planet.

claimResults.note: Matches the NASA planetary fact sheet figure I know (737 K). Rival test: Mercury is closer to the Sun but Venus's greenhouse atmosphere wins; no reading of 'surface, on average' favours Mercury. High-risk number, so it relies on check A's external evidence per memo 18.

evidence.restatement: Mercury's mean surface temperature is about 167 degrees Celsius (440 K), per the NASA fact sheet.

claimResults.note: Mean of a huge day/night swing; the item says mean so no trick. 167 C is the standard published mean. Well below Venus on any figure, so the order cannot flip.

evidence.restatement: Venus's air is mostly CO2 and is very dense, and it holds in heat through a runaway greenhouse effect.

claimResults.note: Atmosphere is about 96.5% carbon dioxide. Textbook.

evidence.restatement: Lead's melting point sits near 327.5 degrees Celsius, under Venus's roughly 464 degree surface.

claimResults.note: 327.5 C is the standard value, so molten lead on Venus's surface is a fair claim.

evidence.restatement: Mercury's sunlit side peaks near 430 C and its night side falls to about minus 180 C because it has only a trace exosphere.

claimResults.note: NASA Mercury page gives 430 C / -180 C. 'Almost no atmosphere' is right (exosphere).
